paragraphs: It has always been observed that the habit of legal business does not make men fit to exercise administrative authority. The Americans have borrowed from the English, their forefathers, an institution unknown on the continent of Europe: I mean the Justices of the Peace. The Justice of the Peace is a kind of middle term between the magistrate and the ordinary man of the world, between the civil officer and the judge. A justice of the peace is a well-informed citizen, though not necessarily trained in the law. His office simply requires him to carry out the police regulations of society, a task in which good sense and integrity are worth more than legal science. The justice brings into the administration a certain taste for established forms and for publicity, which makes him a most unserviceable instrument of despotism. On the other hand, he is not blinded by the superstitions that make legal officers unfit members of a government. The Americans have adopted the English system of justices of the peace, but they have stripped it of the aristocratic character that is visible in the mother country. The Governor of Massachusetts *p appoints a certain number of justices of the peace in every county, and their terms last seven years. *q He also picks three individuals from the whole body of justices, and these form in each county what is called the Court of Sessions. The justices take a personal share in public business. Sometimes they are given administrative functions alongside elected officers, *r and sometimes they form a tribunal before which the magistrates summarily prosecute a refractory citizen, or the citizens report abuses by the magistrate. But it is in the Court of Sessions that they exercise their most important functions. This court meets twice a year in the county town; in Massachusetts it has the power to enforce the obedience of most *s public officers. *t It must be noted that in the State of Massachusetts the Court of Sessions is at once an administrative body, properly so called, and a political tribunal. It has been claimed that the county is a purely administrative division. The Court of Sessions oversees the small number of affairs that concern several townships, or all the townships of the county in common, and so cannot be entrusted to any one of them in particular. *u In all that concerns county business, the duties of the Court of Sessions are purely administrative; and if in its investigations it occasionally borrows the forms of judicial procedure, it does so only to inform itself, *v or as a guarantee to the community over which it presides. But when the administration of the township is brought before it, it always acts as a judicial body, and in a few cases as an official assembly.
p [ We shall learn later what a Governor is. I will content myself here with noting that he represents the executive power of the whole State.]
q [ See the Constitution of Massachusetts, chap. II. sect. 1. Section 9; chap. III. Section 3.]

r [ Thus, for example, a stranger arrives in a township from a country where a contagious disease prevails, and he falls ill. Two justices of the peace can, with the assent of the selectmen, order the sheriff of the county to remove him and look after him.—Act of June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 540.

In general the justices take part in all the important acts of the administration and give them a semi-judicial character.] [Footnote s: I say most, because certain administrative misdemeanors are brought before ordinary tribunals. If, for instance, a township refuses to make the necessary expenditure for its schools or to name a school committee, it is liable to a heavy fine. But this penalty is pronounced by the Supreme Judicial Court or the Court of Common Pleas. See Act of March 10, 1827, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. iii. p. 190. The same is true when a township neglects to provide the necessary war supplies.—Act of February 21, 1822: Id., vol. ii. p. 570.]

t [ In their individual capacity the justices of the peace take part in the business of the counties and townships.] [Footnote u: These affairs can be grouped under the following heads:—1. The building of prisons and courthouses. 2. The county budget, which is afterward voted by the State. 3. The distribution of the taxes so voted. 4. The granting of certain patents. 5. The laying out and repair of the county roads.]
v [ Thus, when a road is under consideration, almost all difficulties are settled with the help of the jury.]

The first difficulty is to secure the obedience of an authority as entirely independent of the general laws of the State as the township is. We have said that assessors are named every year by the town meetings to levy the taxes. If a township tries to evade payment of the taxes by neglecting to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions sentences it to a heavy penalty. *w The fine is levied on each of the inhabitants, and the sheriff of the county, who is the officer of justice, carries out the order. In this way, in the United States, the authority of the government is mysteriously hidden under the forms of a judicial sentence, and at the same time its influence is strengthened by the irresistible power with which people have invested the formalities of law.
w [ See Act of February 20, 1786, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 217.]

These proceedings are easy to follow and to understand. The demands made on a township are in general plain and exactly defined; they consist of a simple fact without any complication, or of a principle without detailed application. *x But the difficulty grows when what must be enforced is not the obedience of the township but that of the town officers. All the blameworthy actions of which a public official may be guilty can be reduced to the following heads:

x [ There is an indirect method of enforcing the obedience of a township. Suppose that the funds the law requires for the upkeep of the roads have not been voted. The town surveyor is then authorized, ex officio, to raise the money. Since he is personally liable to private individuals for the state of the roads, and can be indicted before the Court of Sessions, he is sure to use the extraordinary right the law gives him against the township. Thus, by threatening the officer, the Court of Sessions extracts compliance from the town. See Act of March 5, 1787, Id., vol. i. p. 305.]
He may carry out the law without energy or zeal;
He may neglect to carry out the law;
He may do what the law forbids him to do.

Only the last two violations of duty can come before a tribunal; a positive and measurable fact is the indispensable foundation of an action at law. Thus, if the selectmen fail to fulfill the legal formalities customary at town elections, they may be sentenced to pay a fine; *y but when the public officer performs his duty without ability, and when he obeys the letter of the law without zeal or energy, he is at least beyond the reach of judicial interference. In this case the Court of Sessions, even when it is acting with its full official powers, cannot compel him to a more satisfactory obedience. The fear of removal is the only check on these quasi-offences; and as the Court of Sessions does not create the town authorities, it cannot remove officials it does not appoint. Moreover, a perpetual investigation would be needed to convict the officer of negligence or lukewarmness, and the Court of Sessions sits only twice a year and judges only the offences brought to its attention. The only security for that active and enlightened obedience, which a court of justice cannot impose on public officers, lies in the possibility of removing them at will. In France this security is sought in powers exercised by the heads of the administration; in America it is sought in the principle of election.
y [ Laws of Massachusetts, vol. ii. p. 45.]

Thus, to sum up in a few words what I have been showing: if a public officer in New England commits a crime in the exercise of his functions, the ordinary courts of justice are always called on to pass sentence on him. If he commits a fault in his official capacity, a purely administrative tribunal is empowered to punish him; and if the matter is important or urgent, the judge makes up for the officer’s omission. *z Lastly, if the same individual is guilty of one of those intangible offences of which human justice takes no notice, he appears every year before a tribunal from which there is no appeal, which can at once reduce him to insignificance and take away his office. This system undoubtedly has great advantages, but carrying it out involves a practical difficulty that is important to point out.

z [ If, for instance, a township persists in refusing to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions appoints them, and the magistrates so appointed have the same authority as elected officers. See the Act quoted above, February 20, 1787.]

I have already observed that the administrative tribunal called the Court of Sessions has no right of inspection over the town officers. It can intervene only when the conduct of a magistrate is specifically brought to its attention, and this is the delicate part of the system. The Americans of New England do not have the office of public prosecutor in the Court of Sessions, *a and it is easy to see that it could not have been established without difficulty. If an accusing magistrate had been appointed only in the chief town of each county, with no agents to help him in the townships, he would have known no more of what was going on in the county than the members of the Court of Sessions. But to appoint agents in each township would have been to concentrate in his person the most formidable of powers, that of a judicial administration. Moreover, laws are the children of habit, and nothing of the kind exists in the legislation of England. The Americans have therefore divided the offices of inspection and prosecution, as they have divided all the other functions of the administration. Grand jurors are required by law to inform the court to which they belong of all the misdemeanors committed in their county. *b There are certain great offences that are prosecuted officially by the States; *c but more often the task of punishing offenders falls to the fiscal officer, whose duty it is to receive the fine. Thus the treasurer of the township is charged with prosecuting such administrative offences as come to his notice. But American legislation makes a more particular appeal to the private interest of the citizen; *d and this great principle is constantly met with in studying the laws of the United States. American legislators are more ready to credit men with intelligence than with honesty, and they rely not a little on personal greed for the execution of the laws. When an individual is really and perceptibly injured by an administrative abuse, it is natural that his personal interest should lead him to prosecute. But if a legal formality is required that, however advantageous to the community, matters little to individuals, plaintiffs may be harder to find; and thus, by a tacit agreement, the laws may fall into disuse. Brought by their system to this extremity, the Americans are obliged to encourage informers by giving them a share of the penalty in certain cases, *e and to ensure the execution of the laws by the dangerous expedient of degrading the morals of the people. The only administrative authority above the county magistrates is, properly speaking, that of the government.
a [ I say the Court of Sessions, because in common courts there is a magistrate who exercises some of the functions of a public prosecutor.]
b [ The grand-jurors are, for instance, bound to inform the court of the bad state of the roads.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 308.]

c [ If, for instance, the treasurer of the county holds back his accounts.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 406.] [Footnote d: Thus, if a private individual suffers a breakdown or is injured because of the bad state of a road, he can sue the township or the county for damages at the sessions.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 309.]

e [ In cases of invasion or insurrection, if the town officers neglect to furnish the necessary stores and ammunition for the militia, the township may be sentenced to a fine of from $200 to $500. One can easily imagine that in such a case no one might care to prosecute; hence the law adds that any citizen may bring an indictment for offences of this kind, and that half of the fine shall go to the plaintiff. See Act of March 6, 1810, vol. ii. p. 236. The same clause is frequently found in the law of Massachusetts. Private individuals are not only encouraged in this way to prosecute public officers; public officers are likewise encouraged to bring the disobedience of private individuals to justice. If a citizen refuses to do the work assigned to him on a road, the road surveyor may prosecute him, and he receives half the penalty for himself. See the Laws cited above, vol. i. p. 308.]

General Remarks on the Administration of the United States Differences among the States of the Union in their systems of administration—Activity and perfection of the local authorities decrease toward the South—Power of the magistrate increases; that of the elector diminishes—Administration passes from the township to the county—States of New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania—Principles of administration applicable to the whole Union—Election of public officers, and inalienability of their functions—Absence of gradation of ranks—Introduction of judicial resources into the administration.

I have already said that after examining in detail the constitution of the township and the county in New England, I would take a general view of the rest of the Union. Townships and local activity exist in every State; but nowhere in the confederation is there a township exactly like those of New England. The farther south we go, the less active the business of the township or parish becomes; the number of magistrates, functions, and rights decreases; the population has a less direct influence on affairs; town meetings are less frequent, and the subjects of debate fewer. The power of the elected magistrate grows and that of the elector shrinks, while the public spirit of the local communities is less awake and less influential. *f These differences can be seen to some extent in the State of New York; they are very noticeable in Pennsylvania; but they become less striking as we move toward the northwest. Most of the emigrants who settle in the northwestern States are natives of New England, and they carry the habits of their mother country into the one they adopt. A township in Ohio is by no means unlike a township in Massachusetts.
f [ For details see the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. pp. 336-364, entitled, “Of the Powers, Duties, and Privileges of Towns.”

See in the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, the words Assessors, Collector, Constables, Overseer of the Poor, Supervisors of Highways; and in the Acts of a general nature of the State of Ohio, the Act of February 25, 1834, relating to townships, p. 412; besides the particular provisions relating to various town officers, such as Township’s Clerk, Trustees, Overseers of the Poor, Fence Viewers, Appraisers of Property, Township’s Treasurer, Constables, Supervisors of Highways.]

We have seen that in Massachusetts the mainspring of public administration lies in the township. It is the common center of the citizens’ interests and affections. But this ceases to be so as we move down to States where knowledge is less widely spread, and where the township therefore offers fewer guarantees of a wise and active administration. As we leave New England, then, we find that the importance of the town passes gradually to the county, which becomes the center of administration and the intermediate power between the government and the citizen. In Massachusetts the business of the county is conducted by the Court of Sessions, made up of a quorum named by the Governor and his council; but the county has no representative assembly, and its expenditure is voted by the national legislature. In the great State of New York, by contrast, and in Ohio and Pennsylvania, the inhabitants of each county choose a certain number of representatives, who form the assembly of the county. *g The county assembly has the right to tax the inhabitants to a certain extent, and in this respect it has the privileges of a real legislative body. At the same time it exercises executive power in the county, often directs the administration of the townships, and confines their authority within much narrower limits than in Massachusetts.

g [ See the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. p. 340. Id. chap. xii. p. 366; also in the Acts of the State of Ohio, an act relating to county commissioners, February 25, 1824, p. 263. See the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, at the words County-rates and Levies, p. 170. In the State of New York each township elects a representative, who takes part in the administration of the county as well as in that of the township.]

Those are the main differences between the systems of county and town administration in the Federal States. If I meant to examine American law in minute detail, I would have to point out still more differences in how the several communities carry out their business. But what I have said is enough to show the general principles on which administration in the United States rests. These principles are applied in different ways, and they produce more or fewer consequences from place to place, but they remain substantially the same. The laws differ and their outward features change; their character does not. The township and the county are not set up the same way everywhere, yet in the United States both always rest on one principle: each person is the best judge of what concerns himself alone, and the best person to meet his own private needs. So the township and the county must look after their own special interests. The State governs, but it does not interfere in how they administer them. We may find exceptions to this rule, but never a contrary principle.

The first consequence of this doctrine has been that all the magistrates are chosen either by the citizens or at least from among them. Since the officers are everywhere elected or appointed for a fixed period, it has been impossible to set up the rules of a dependent chain of authorities; there are almost as many independent officials as there are functions, and the executive power is scattered among a multitude of hands. Hence arose the indispensable necessity of bringing the administration under the control of the courts of justice, together with the system of pecuniary penalties by which the secondary bodies and their representatives are forced to obey the laws. This system prevails from one end of the Union to the other. The power to punish the misconduct of public officers, or to act as the executive in urgent cases, has not, however, been given to the same judges in all the States. The Anglo-Americans took the institution of justices of the peace from a common source; but although it exists in all the States, it is not always put to the same use. The justices of the peace everywhere take part in the administration of the townships and the counties, *h either as public officers or as judges of public misdemeanors, but in most of the States the more important classes of public offences come before the ordinary tribunals.
h [ In some of the Southern States the county courts are charged with all the details of the administration. See the Statutes of the State of Tennessee, arts. Judiciary, Taxes, etc.]

Election of public officers, or the inalienability of their functions; the absence of any gradation of powers; judicial control over the secondary branches of the administration: these are the features found everywhere in the American system, from Maine to the Floridas. In some States traces of a centralized administration begin to show, and New York has gone furthest in this direction. In New York the officers of the central government sometimes exercise a kind of inspection or control over the secondary bodies. *i

i [ For instance, the direction of public instruction is centered in the hands of the government. The legislature names the members of the University, who are called Regents; the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor of the State are necessarily among them.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455. The Regents of the University visit the colleges and academies every year and report to the legislature. Their supervision is not ineffective, for several reasons: colleges, in order to become corporations, need a charter, which is granted only on the recommendation of the Regents; every year funds are distributed by the State to encourage learning, and the Regents distribute this money. See chap. xv. “Instruction,” Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455.
The school commissioners are required to send an annual report to the Superintendent of the Republic.—Id. p. 488.
A similar report is made every year to the same person on the number and condition of the poor.—Id. p. 631.]

At other times they form a court of appeal for deciding affairs. *j In the State of New York judicial penalties are used less than elsewhere as a means of administration, and the right to prosecute the offences of public officers is placed in fewer hands. *k The same tendency can be faintly seen in some other States; *l but in general the most prominent feature of administration in the United States is its excessive local independence.

j [ If anyone believes himself wronged by the school commissioners (who are town officers), he can appeal to the superintendent of the primary schools, whose decision is final.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 487.

Provisions similar to those cited above are found from time to time in the laws of the State of New York; but in general these attempts at centralization are weak and unproductive. The great authorities of the State have the right to watch and control the subordinate agents, but not to reward or punish them. The same individual is never empowered both to give an order and to punish disobedience; he therefore has the right to command without the means of exacting compliance. In 1830 the Superintendent of Schools complained in his Annual Report to the legislature that several school commissioners had neglected, despite his request, to send him the accounts that were due. He added that if this omission continued, he would be obliged to prosecute them, as the law directs, before the proper tribunals.]
k [ Thus the district attorney is directed to recover all fines below the sum of fifty dollars, unless that right has been specially given to another magistrate.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 383.]

l [ Several traces of centralization can be found in Massachusetts; for instance, the committees of the town schools are directed to make an annual report to the Secretary of State. See Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 367.]

I have described the townships and the administration; it now remains for me to speak of the State and the government. I can pass over this ground quickly without fear of being misunderstood, for everything I have to say is found in the written forms of the various constitutions, which are easy to obtain. These constitutions rest on a simple and rational theory; their forms have been adopted by all constitutional nations and have become familiar to us. Here, therefore, I need only give a short analysis; I shall try afterward to pass judgment on what I now describe.
Legislative Power of the State
Division of the Legislative Body into Two Houses—Senate—House of Representatives—Different Functions of These Two Bodies.

The legislative power of the State rests in two assemblies; the first usually carries the name of Senate. The Senate is normally a legislative body, but at times it also acts as an executive and judicial one. How it takes part in government varies with the constitutions of the different States; *m but it most often exercises executive power in nominating public officers. It shares in judicial power when certain political offences are tried, and sometimes when certain civil cases are decided. *n It always has few members. The other branch of the legislature, usually called the House of Representatives, has no share at all in the administration. It takes part in judicial power only by impeaching public officers before the Senate. Almost everywhere the members of the two Houses are subject to the same conditions of election, and are chosen in the same way by the same citizens. The one difference between them is that senators are generally chosen for a longer term than representatives. Representatives seldom stay in office more than a year; senators usually sit two or three years. Because senators may be chosen for several years and are renewed in rotation, the law keeps in the legislative body a nucleus of men who are already used to public business and who can have a salutary influence on the junior members.
m [ In Massachusetts the Senate is not invested with any administrative functions.]
n [ As in the State of New York.]

The Americans plainly did not intend, by dividing the legislative body into two branches, to make one house hereditary and the other elected, one aristocratic and the other democratic. It was not their purpose to create in the one a bulwark of power while the other represented the interests and passions of the people. The only advantages that result from the present constitution of the United States are the division of the legislative power and the resulting check on political assemblies, together with the creation of a tribunal of appeal for the revision of the laws.

Time and experience, however, have convinced the Americans that, even if these are its only advantages, dividing the legislative power is still a principle of the greatest necessity. Pennsylvania was the only one of the United States that at first tried to set up a single House of Assembly. Franklin himself was so swept along by the necessary consequences of the principle of the sovereignty of the people that he went along with it. But the Pennsylvanians soon had to change the law and create two Houses. So the principle of dividing the legislative power was finally established, and its necessity can now be regarded as a demonstrated truth. The republics of antiquity hardly knew this theory. It entered the world almost by accident, as so many other great truths have, and several modern nations have misunderstood it. At last it has become an axiom of the political science of our age.
[See Benjamin Franklin]
The Executive Power of the State
Office of Governor in an American State—The place he occupies in relation to the legislature—His rights and his duties—His dependence on the people.

The executive power of the State may truly be said to be represented by the Governor, although he holds only a portion of its rights. The supreme magistrate, under the title of Governor, is the official moderator and counselor of the legislature. He is armed with a veto, or suspensive power, which allows him to stop, or at least to delay, its movements at will. He lays the needs of the country before the legislative body and points out the means he thinks may usefully be employed to meet them; he is the natural executor of its decrees in all undertakings that concern the nation at large. *o When the legislature is not in session, the Governor is bound to take all necessary steps to guard the State against violent shocks and unforeseen dangers. The whole military power of the State is at the Governor’s disposal. He is the commander of the militia and head of the armed force. When the authority that is by general consent granted to the laws is disregarded, the Governor puts himself at the head of the armed force of the State to put down resistance and restore order. Lastly, the Governor takes no share in the administration of townships and counties, except indirectly through the nomination of Justices of the Peace, a nomination he has no power to cancel. *p The Governor is an elected magistrate, generally chosen for only one or two years, so that he always remains strictly dependent on the majority that elected him.

o [ In practice, it is not always the Governor who carries out the plans of the legislature; it often happens that the legislature, in voting a measure, names special agents to oversee its execution.]
p [ In some of the States the justices of the peace are not chosen by the Governor.]
Political Effects of the System of Local Administration in the United States

Necessary distinction between the general centralization of government and the centralization of the local administration—Local administration not centralized in the United States: great general centralization of the government—Some bad consequences resulting to the United States from the local administration—Administrative advantages of this order of things—The power that conducts the government is less regular, less enlightened, less learned, but much greater than in Europe—Political advantages of this order of things—In the United States the interests of the country are everywhere kept in view—Support given to the government by the community—Provincial institutions more necessary as the social condition becomes more democratic—Reason for this.

Centralization has become a word in general and daily use, without any precise meaning attached to it. Nevertheless, there are two distinct kinds of centralization, which must be carefully told apart. Certain interests are common to all parts of a nation, such as the enactment of its general laws and the maintenance of its foreign relations. Other interests are particular to certain parts of the nation, such as the business of different townships. When the power that directs the general interests is gathered in one place, or vested in the same persons, it constitutes a central government. In the same way, the power of directing partial or local interests, when brought together in one place, constitutes what may be called a central administration.

On some points these two kinds of centralization merge; but by classifying the matters that fall more particularly within the province of each, we can easily tell them apart. Clearly, a central government gains immense power when it is united with administrative centralization. Combined in this way, it accustoms men to set their own will aside habitually and completely, to submit not just once or on one point, but in every respect and at all times. This union of power therefore not only subdues them by compulsion; it also affects them in the ordinary habits of life and influences each individual, first separately and then collectively.

These two kinds of centralization help and attract each other, but they must not be thought inseparable. It is impossible to imagine a more completely central government than the one that existed in France under Louis XIV. When the same individual was the author and interpreter of the laws and the representative of France at home and abroad, he was justified in claiming that the State was identified with his person. Nevertheless, the administration was much less centralized under Louis XIV than it is today.

In England the centralization of the government is carried to great perfection. The State has the compact vigor of a single man; by an act of its will alone it sets immense machinery in motion and wields or gathers the efforts of its authority. Indeed, I cannot conceive that a nation can have a secure or prosperous existence without a powerful centralization of government. But I think that a central administration saps the strength of the nations in which it exists, because it constantly weakens their public spirit. Such an administration may succeed, at a given moment and at a given point, in gathering all the available resources of a people. Even so, it at least harms the renewal of those resources. It may secure victory in the hour of struggle, but it slowly loosens the sinews of strength. It can do wonders for the passing greatness of one man; it cannot ensure the lasting prosperity of a nation.

If we look carefully, we shall find that whenever people say a State cannot act because it has no central point, what it lacks is centralization of government. People often claim, and we are ready to believe, that the German empire never managed to bring all its powers into action. The reason was that the State could never enforce obedience to its general laws. The several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, to refuse their cooperation to the representatives of the common authority, even in matters that concerned the mass of the people. In other words, there was no centralization of government. The same remark applies to the Middle Ages. All the confusion of feudal society came from this: control over general interests, as well as local ones, was divided among a thousand hands and broken up in a thousand ways. Without a central government, the nations of Europe could not move energetically along any straight course.

We have shown that the United States has no central administration and no dependent chain of public officials. Local authority has been pushed to lengths that no European nation could tolerate without great inconvenience, and that have even had some harmful results in America. But in the United States the centralization of the government is complete, and it would be easy to prove that the national power is more compact than it has ever been in the old nations of Europe. Each State has only one legislative body and only one source of political authority. District assemblies and county courts have generally not been multiplied, for fear that they might be tempted to go beyond their administrative duties and interfere with the government. In America the legislature of each State is supreme. Nothing can impede its authority: not privileges, not local immunities, not personal influence, not even the empire of reason, since the legislature represents the majority, which claims to be the sole organ of reason. Its own decision is therefore the only limit on its action. Beside it, and under its immediate control, stands the representative of the executive power, whose duty is to make the refractory submit by superior force. The only sign of weakness lies in certain details of how the government acts. The American republics have no standing armies to intimidate a discontented minority; but no minority has yet been driven to declare open war, so the need for an army has not been felt. *q The State usually uses the officers of the township or the county to deal with the citizens. Thus, in New England, the assessor sets the rate of taxes, the collector receives them, the town treasurer sends the amount to the public treasury, and any disputes that arise go before the ordinary courts of justice. This way of collecting taxes is slow as well as inconvenient, and it would be a permanent hindrance to a government with large financial demands. In whatever materially affects its existence, the government ought to be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at will, and used to rapid methods of proceeding. But it will always be easy for the central government, organized as it is in America, to introduce new and more effective ways of acting, suited to its needs. [Footnote q: [The Civil War of 1860-65 cruelly belied this statement, and in the course of the struggle the North alone called two and a half million men to arms; but to the honor of the United States it must be added that, when the contest ended, this army disappeared as rapidly as it had been raised.—Translator’s Note.]]
